title: Making tax simpler—or adding more work?
label: 12 November 2026 · Tax administration
summary: Rebecca Benneyworth, an accountant and member of the Administrative Burdens Advisory Board, said that requiring employers to report employee benefits through payroll could simplify tax—but only if it asks for limited information. She warned that the planned system demands more detail and more regular work, especially from small businesses, and may strain HMRC’s payroll systems. She supported a proposed way for taxpayers to correct errors, while raising concerns about the meaning of “reckless” and the reliability of HMRC’s estimate of unpaid tax. She called for clearer guidance, careful review of the new systems, and greater scrutiny of how the tax gap is calculated.

chapters.title: A simpler idea, a more complicated system
chapters.takeaway: Benneyworth supports taxing employee benefits through payroll but says the planned reporting rules demand far more information than the existing voluntary system.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Could you explain the role of the Administrative Burdens Advisory Board and why you’ve criticised the new rules for taxing employee benefits through payroll?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: I’m a chartered accountant with a small practice serving small businesses. The board is made up of volunteers with business experience. We act as a critical friend to HMRC: we examine how tax policies work in practice, suggest ways to simplify them, and report to the minister.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: We support the aim. Under the old system, employers report benefits after the tax year. With payrolling, the taxable value is added to an employee’s pay as the year goes along. That should make tax more accurate and transparent, and could make things simpler.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: But employers have been able to do this voluntarily for about 10 years, and we expected that system to lead into the compulsory one. We encouraged clients to try it early. Instead, the mandatory system looks very different.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What’s different about it?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: The proposed reporting rules ask for much more detailed information than voluntary payrolling. With a company car worth £2,400 in taxable benefits, the simple approach is to add £200 to the employee’s pay each month and tax it.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: The new rules would require details for different kinds of benefits, both for each pay period and as a running total. We don’t know exactly why HMRC needs all that. It may be to help check compliance, but I can only speculate.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: After concerns from our board and software companies, the start was delayed and the rollout split into stages. From April 2027, cars, vans, fuel and medical benefits are due to be included. Other benefits are planned for 2028, with some difficult cases treated separately.

turns.speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
turns.text: Why might HMRC need so much information?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: To calculate the tax, you mainly need the value of the benefit for that month. If the system only asked for that figure, we’d see it as a real simplification. The original proposal asked employers to report each benefit separately, which seems to go beyond what’s needed to calculate the tax.

chapters.title: The extra work for employers and payroll systems
chapters.takeaway: Even when a payroll agent does the calculations, small employers must regularly collect, check and pass on changing information.

turns.speaker: Lord Leigh of Hurley
turns.text: If a business uses an outside payroll agent, is this really much extra work? Cars don’t change often, and insurance premiums are just figures from the insurer.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: It depends on the business, but the employer still has to gather the information and get it to the agent on time. A medical insurance bill, for example, may need to be divided among employees, and the amount can change when someone adds a family member.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: I have clients who forget to tell us when something changes, even under the voluntary system. We sometimes discover at year-end that an employee was given a van months earlier. Making the reporting monthly means employers need to keep track throughout the year.

turns.speaker: Lord Leigh of Hurley
turns.text: But for a company with only a few employees, would those changes really add much work?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: A small company might start a medical insurance plan and then have to notice when premiums change, check which employees are affected and tell its agent. For a company with 50, 60 or 200 employees, splitting the costs and keeping up with changes is a continuing task.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: Could this be an HMRC attempt to make benefits too difficult for small businesses to offer?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: I don’t think so. It wouldn’t make sense for tax revenue: if an employer didn’t provide a work van, the employee might need to use their own vehicle and receive a tax-free mileage payment. HMRC’s proper aim is to collect the right tax when people receive wages or a benefit.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: Will some employers end up using the new monthly system for certain benefits and the old year-end form for others?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: Yes. Some benefits, such as accommodation, can be difficult to value monthly, and employers may still have to report them after the year. HMRC is also encouraging employers to put some other benefits through payroll voluntarily, so an employer could be dealing with two different processes.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: For a small business, running two systems is more administration, not less.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bi
turns.text: Is there a risk that the digital change is moving faster than HMRC’s systems and the software employers use?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: Yes. Policy, HMRC’s computer systems and commercial payroll software all develop at different speeds. I’m concerned the amount of extra information could put too much pressure on RTI, which already has problems.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: Software companies also have a lot to build, including software for Making Tax Digital. The delay gave HMRC more time to respond to concerns, but we’ll only know how well the new system works once it’s in use.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bi
turns.text: We’ve heard that RTI has had millions of pounds’ worth of mismatches, with some cases automatically sent to debt management. Could extra reporting make that worse?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: That’s a valid concern. Payroll professionals often find that information they’ve sent is recorded differently by HMRC. Those problems are being addressed, but more information passing through the system could increase the risk of mismatches.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: The board would strongly recommend reviewing the costs and results a year or two after the changes begin. HMRC should check whether the system delivered the hoped-for savings or whether it underestimated employers’ extra costs.

chapters.title: Helping people put tax mistakes right
chapters.takeaway: Benneyworth supports a chance to correct apparent errors without a penalty, but says clearer guidance and careful handling of the proposed “reckless” standard are essential.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What do you think of the proposed system for correcting tax errors?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: HMRC estimates that a large share of unpaid tax is linked to small businesses, but my experience is mostly with businesses that use an adviser, so it may not represent everyone. Most small businesses want to pay the right amount, but they can get confused or fail to keep good records.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: A notice to correct could be useful. If HMRC spots something that appears wrong, it could contact the business or its adviser and ask them to correct it or explain why it’s right. That may be quicker and cheaper than a long investigation.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: The proposal gives the taxpayer a period to fix the problem, though the exact time isn’t clear. If they correct it, there would be no penalty even if the original mistake was careless. If they ignore the notice, the error would be treated as deliberate.

turns.speaker: Lord Newby
turns.text: Could HMRC do more to explain tax rules and make them simpler? The tax system itself can be a source of mistakes.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: Poor record-keeping is a major cause. Some people leave their records until they’re a jumble of receipts, and neither they nor their accountant can work out what happened. Making Tax Digital should help many people keep better records.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: Simplifying tax is difficult because small changes can create unfairness or cost the public money. Even whether a cup of coffee counts as a business expense can depend on the circumstances. There isn’t always a simple rule that works fairly for everyone.

turns.speaker: Lord Leigh of Hurley
turns.text: Does HMRC understand what small businesses need, and what more could it do?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: Some parts of HMRC understand small businesses well; I’m less sure that understanding reaches every part of its compliance work. It should keep producing clear, practical guides for situations such as starting a business or hiring a first employee.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: Good guidance should use decision charts and realistic examples, not just state the obvious. HMRC’s Tax Confident materials are a promising start, and the board supports doing more of that.

turns.speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
turns.text: Will ordinary taxpayers and HMRC staff understand the difference between a careless mistake and a reckless one?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: I’m not sure. The system used to distinguish between mistakes made despite reasonable care, careless mistakes and deliberate ones. “Reckless” is a more subjective judgment, and I can’t yet say exactly how it will differ from deliberate.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: That makes training important, especially as HMRC is recruiting many new staff. The judgment will need experience and oversight. Tax advisers and professional bodies can help explain the rules, but not every business can afford an adviser, and there aren’t enough advisers for that to be the answer.

turns.speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
turns.text: Is this mainly a way for the Government to raise money by closing the tax gap?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: I expect it’s partly intended to reduce the tax gap, but I don’t think the “reckless” measure will raise a great deal by itself. It may discourage people from taking risks, and there may be some high-profile cases. I’m not convinced the tax gap figures reflect what’s happening in small businesses.

chapters.title: How much tax is really going unpaid?
chapters.takeaway: Benneyworth thinks small businesses may account for a substantial amount of unpaid tax, but questions whether HMRC’s estimate is too high and cautions against dismissing a practical correction threshold.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: Some people say HMRC’s estimate of unpaid tax is unreliable and is being used to justify policy. Should outsiders examine how it’s calculated?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: Yes, although it would need careful handling. HMRC uses different methods, including estimates based on the results of checks on businesses. If the number of cases checked is too small, the estimate could be wrong in either direction.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: I suspect the small-business estimate may be too high. A business might agree to pay a disputed amount because continuing to argue would cost more than the tax at stake. That could make the figures look as if more tax was wrongly unpaid, even when the business simply couldn’t justify its position to HMRC.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: I still think a substantial part of unpaid tax may come from small businesses, but I’m not sure it’s the roughly two-thirds HMRC suggests. Even a smaller share would be worth addressing.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: The National Audit Office might be able to examine the figures, but it would need tax expertise and HMRC might have to share sensitive information about how it chooses cases. That makes outside scrutiny difficult.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Could more education help people pay correctly without relying on investigations?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: Yes. I’d like to see more practical material like Tax Confident. There can also be problems when someone runs a small company but doesn’t understand that the company’s money and their own money are legally and financially different.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: An adviser can help, but anyone can call themselves an accountant or tax adviser; those titles aren’t legally protected. Some people helping small firms may not have enough knowledge, which can add to the problem.

turns.speaker: Lord Newby
turns.text: Should HMRC ignore mistakes when only a small amount of tax is involved?

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: I can see the practical case for a minimum amount, because chasing a tiny sum can cost HMRC and a business more than it’s worth. But people whose tax is taken directly from their wages through PAYE don’t get the same leeway, so a cut-off could be unfair.

turns.speaker: Lord Newby
turns.text: That might depend on where the threshold is set.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Benneyworth
turns.text: Yes, it would.
